title: OpenAI releases BioBasicsBench — 100 wet-lab tasks for AI agents
subtitle: Built with enzyme-design company Ligo, the benchmark tests whether AI agents can interpret gel images, colony plates, and raw instrument readouts across five areas of experimental biology. GPT-6 Astra posted a 66.7% mean reward at its highest reasoning setting.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI published BioBasicsBench on November 6, a benchmark of 100 tasks drawn from real experimental biology work and designed to test whether AI agents can handle routine wet-lab science. The benchmark was built with Ligo, a biotech focused on enzyme design, and covers five areas: protein methods, imaging and cytometry, quantification and assays, nucleic acid methods, and molecular cloning. Inputs are the raw artifacts of day-to-day lab work — gel images, colony plates, microscopy frames, instrument readouts — rather than curated figures from publications. Grading is done against rubric criteria that award partial credit, so a mostly correct interpretation is scored differently from a fully correct one. Across the seven models tested, GPT-6 Astra posted a 66.7% mean reward at its highest reasoning setting, against 43.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol. OpenAI's own summary notes that the newer models show real gains in multimodal interpretation and control recognition, but still over-interpret and miscount — in one colony-counting task, Astra overcounted by roughly 12%.

The benchmark closes a gap in how biology-capable AI gets measured. Prior biology benchmarks have leaned on multiple-choice knowledge questions or on polished figures from published papers — closer to a textbook exam than lab work. BioBasicsBench scores the task biology actually looks like most days: open a file, read what the instrument said, decide whether it worked, decide what went wrong if it didn't. That is where agentic AI systems will either integrate into real research or wash out, and it is also where safety considerations get concrete. OpenAI says higher scores do not yet translate to reliable laboratory judgment, and that the benchmark will be used to track biosafety and biosecurity implications as models improve.

The sponsor choice is instructive. Ligo is an enzyme-design company whose actual engineers evaluated the model outputs, giving the benchmark grounded ground truth rather than a crowdsourced or synthetic rubric. That pattern — frontier lab plus a specialist industry partner building the eval together — is becoming the common shape of credible domain benchmarks, and it works because the specialist can tell when an answer is subtly wrong in ways a non-expert grader would miss. Expect more benchmarks of this shape across chemistry, radiology, materials, and law over the next year.

A takeaway for learners: if you are considering biology or any specialized domain, the question to ask about an AI tool is not 'can it pass the exam' but 'can it read my raw data, tell me when the experiment failed, and tell me why.' Benchmarks like BioBasicsBench matter because they measure the second question. If you want to develop good judgment about AI's real capability curve, read evaluation papers and look specifically at the error cases — the 12% overcount is more informative than the 66.7% headline.
